newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries idle in London ahead of sales data.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries idle in London ahead of sales data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were stalled in early London trade on Thursday as retail sales data due later in the session kept investors sidelined, traders said.
They said the rebound in the dollar provided a positive backdrop to the market, but added limited scope for further gains in the greenback would check any positive sentiment.
"The rise in the dollar should be helpful for the market today, but I wouldn't get too carried away," said Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Futures in London.

By 0943 GMT, the 30-year T-bond was at 97-11 to yield 6.83 percent, unchanged from Tokyo and up from 97-08 at the New York close. Ten-year paper was at 100-14, also unchanged from Tokyo and up from 100-12 in New York.

The dollar was at 114.07/17 against the yen, up from 111.20/25 late Wednesday in Europe. It got a boost after Eisuke Sakakibara from the Japanese Ministry of Finance said the nation's trade surplus was not a cause for concern.
But the currency moves failed to stir much interest in Treasuries.
"It's a big yawn in the market today," said one trader. "The way it's going is that there's a flurry of activity after a big number, then everyone blames the next number for not doing anything."
Analysts said May retail sales data due at 1230 GMT was keeping a lid on trade on Thursday.
Tyson was expecting a 0.2 percent rise in the headline rate and a 0.1 percent rise in core, slightly less than the 0.4 percent and 0.3 percent consensus estimates.

"We're looking for some bounce back from the depressed levels in April (sales), but a full recovery is more likely in June," said Tyson. "If anything Treasuries should manage to push a bit higher after the numbers."
The trader said he expected little reaction to the figures, particularly with the producer price data for May due on Friday.
"If the data come in in line there'll be nothing going on, if not, there'll be very, very little effect indeed -- everyone is just marking time," he said.
September T-bond futures were unchanged at 110-19 in automated trade.
